theme: Why should I fear in times of trouble?, Ecclesiastes in the Psalter
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 49. This psalm is a wisdom psalm and a reflection on death and wealth. It is close to Ecclesiastes in tone. Read it as a sermon.
settingTheScene: Psalm 49 is a psalm of the sons of Korah. It begins like a wisdom teacher’s address to all peoples, rich and poor, and it takes up the same problem Ecclesiastes explores: all human beings die, whatever their wealth. It also gives an answer that Ecclesiastes only hints at: God will ransom the faithful from Sheol. It is placed here as the Psalter’s echo of the Preacher.
observation: “Hear this, all peoples! Give ear, all inhabitants of the world, both low and high, rich and poor together!” (vv. 1-2).
“My mouth shall speak wisdom; the meditation of my heart shall be understanding” (v. 3).
“Why should I fear in the days of evil, when the iniquity of my persecutors surrounds me?” (v. 5).
“Truly no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life” (v. 7).
“Man in his pomp will not remain; he is like the beasts that perish” (v. 12).
“Like sheep they are appointed for Sheol; Death shall be their shepherd” (v. 14).
“But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me” (v. 15).
“Be not afraid when a man becomes rich, when the glory of his house increases. For when he dies he will carry nothing away” (vv. 16-17).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with a universal audience. It is not for Israel only but for all the inhabitants of the world. The question it addresses concerns everyone: why fear when the wealthy and powerful seem to have the upper hand? The answer is death. “No man can ransom another.” Not even the richest can buy his way out of the grave. “For he sees that even the wise die.” Wealth, wisdom, and fame all end in the same place.

The psalm describes the false confidence of the wealthy. They name lands after themselves. They trust in their riches and boast of their abundance. But “man in his pomp will not remain.” He is like the beasts. The psalm uses a shocking image: death is their shepherd, leading them like sheep to Sheol. They are being herded, not leading.

Then comes the great turn in verse 15. “But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me.” It is one of the clearest statements of hope beyond death in the Old Testament. The word “ransom” recalls the failure of human ransom in verse 7. No man can ransom another, but God can. And “he will receive me” uses the same verb that was used of Enoch and Elijah being taken by God. It points to a hope of life with God beyond the grave.

The psalm ends with a call not to fear. Do not be afraid when the wicked prosper. They will leave everything behind. Their glory does not follow them. The wise person is not envious of what will be taken away.

This psalm answers the problem of vanity with the hope of ransom. It sees death clearly, but it does not end there.
connection: Jesus said, “The Son of Man came… to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45), the ransom no one else could pay. Paul says, “We brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of it” (1 Timothy 6:7). Hosea 13:14 and 1 Corinthians 15:54-57 speak of victory over Sheol. Jesus told the story of the rich fool (Luke 12:16-21), and said, “What will a man give in return for his soul?” (Mark 8:37).
application:
Do not envy someone who is wealthy. Ask what they will carry with them.

Thank Jesus for being the ransom that no man could pay.

Hold your possessions loosely, knowing that God will receive you.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for giving his life as a ransom for you.
Tell God what you tend to trust in besides him, such as wealth or reputation.
Ask him to loosen your fear of death.
